goal: Decide whether Bend or BendHub packages can make agent-written codelarpers tests and submission checks stricter

extra_axes.name: maintenance
extra_axes.why: the decision is whether to take on third-party packages: their age, upkeep, provenance and the unchecked code they run
extra_axes.ruling_why: every candidate use adds a dependency, and claims about its health decide the outcome

claims.text: BendHub holds 1107 packages, 305 names, 61 authors and 18 posts; the oldest package is from 2026-09-10, so the hub is about two months old.
Only 135 packages (12%) ship LAWS.bend and 136 (12%) PROOF.bend, so 88% carry none of the proofs Bend is pitched on.
257 packages (23%) ship their own .c or .js files, which the API docs say Bend runs without checking; publishing needs no account.

Adoption is concentrated: paymog owns 48 of the 128 names sampled, and 310 of the 322 packages importing the most-imported name (bend-kit-bytes) are bend-kit's own; 730 packages (66%) give no source repository.
The only testing packages are bend-kit-property (property checks with shrinking: 3 files, 0 dependents, 0 mentions, no LAWS or PROOF) and an unnamed 'bendcheck'; a search for 'assert' finds nothing.

bend is not installed here; codelarpers runs stage tests as test.py, test.sh, test.mjs, test.js or an executable test (course.rs:244), and its starter kits are rust, go, python, javascript, typescript, c and cpp, with no Bend.
Bend itself is v2.0.39 and its site says it is still evolving and to expect bugs.
Write stage tests that need generated inputs with bend-kit-property, so a learner's failure shrinks to the smallest input that breaks their program.

evidence.source: bend-kit-property description: reproducible property checks with generated inputs and greedy shrinking

claims.ruling_why: O1, O2 and O4 stand: a new toolchain on every learner's machine for a package nobody imports, when the same benefit fits in the existing Python helper

claims.text: Add a bend starter kit so codelarpers can host courses written in Bend, with hub packages as the libraries learners import and, where they cite a public repo and licence, as tutorial code examples; packages are content-addressed and never change, so an example's URL stays valid.

evidence.source: https://hub.bend-lang.com/guide (packages named by content hash, never change; default licence MIT-0)

claims.ruling_why: Q1: no courses written in Bend

claims.text: Get the same shrinking benefit without Bend: add property checks with greedy shrinking to the embedded Python helper (codelarpers_test), which needs nothing new on the learner's machine.

evidence.source: codelarpers_test already has a seeded random; a greedy shrinker over lists and strings is a small loop

claims.text: Every learner would need the Bend toolchain (curl | sh) and an executable test wrapper just to run stage tests, in courses written in Rust, Python or Go that never otherwise touch Bend.

The ecosystem is two months old and mostly one author's family; the one testing package has no users, and versions churn fast (bend-kit-http is at 0.38 within about six weeks), so a course pinned to a package today is likely pinned to an abandoned one soon.
As code examples, most packages fail the skill's rule of real code someone shipped: 66% name no source repository, authorship cannot be checked, and 23% run unchecked native code.
Shrinking is the only thing P1 adds, and it needs no Bend: the learner-facing gain is a smaller failing input in the log, which the Python helper can produce.
Each authoring agent would have to load Bend's guide before writing a Bend test or course, on top of the course's own research.

evidence.source: bend-lang.com: agents are told to run `bend guide`, which prints the whole language

claims.text: Use hub packages only inside a course that teaches Bend, and only packages that name a public source repository and licence; never in the harness or in other languages' tests.
claims.ruling_why: Q1: no Bend course to host packages in

claims.text: Across the 109 distinct LAWS.bend files on the hub, 2056 of 3552 laws (57%) are general (for x: T, e.g. decrypt(encrypt(b)) == b) and 1496 (42%) are fixed-input equalities proven by computation; 86 files have at least one general law.

evidence.source: fetched every LAWS.bend and PROOF.bend via /0x<hash>/<path>

claims.text: Bend's GUIDE.md, which `bend guide` prints for an agent to learn the language, is 28,495 bytes, about 7k tokens.

Commit f29fa4a makes `dev validate` require near-misses: per stage, solution files with one plausible bug that must pass earlier stages and fail their own on every seed; the wc example now validates across three seeds.

evidence.source: git log f29fa4a; handed-off session report

claims.text: The tester only sees a submission as a process: it runs .codelarpers/run.sh and checks exit code, stdout, stderr and files; nothing reads the submission's source.

For each stage, the authoring agent writes a Bend reference model plus LAWS.bend and proves the laws, then uses the proven model as the oracle that produces expected output for random inputs; J8 shows agents already write and prove general laws on the hub.
claims.ruling_why: O7, O8 and O10 stand: the proof binds the model, not the submission, the oracle role is already filled by independent implementations, and the model needs Bend on every learner's machine or freezes the seeds

claims.text: Take Bend's discipline without Bend: each stage states its laws (general properties such as lines(a+b) = lines(a) + lines(b)), and the Python helper gains law(name, generate, check), which samples seeded inputs against the learner's program, shrinks a failure to the smallest counterexample and prints the law's name; fixed edge cases stay as cases, and near-misses must break a law or a case.

estimate.unit: lines of stdlib Python plus doc changes

evidence.source: J8 (the kinds of laws agents write), J10, J11, cli/src/tester/codelarpers_test.py

claims.text: A Bend proof constrains the Bend model only; the submission is a black-box process (J11), so it is still judged by sampling outputs on chosen inputs, exactly as with any other oracle.

The oracle role is already filled independently: the studied codebase for codebase courses, the real tool for tutorials, and solution/ proven green; a Bend model is a second implementation by the same agent, whose laws come from the same reading of the spec, so a misread spec is proven, not caught.

evidence.source: references/CURRICULUM.md and TESTS.md oracle guidance; SKILL.md step 5

claims.text: Every authoring session would load about 7k tokens of Bend guide before writing a model, then spend more on proofs; 12 of the 109 proof files on the hub were generated by scripts, a hint that proofs at scale need tooling.

estimate.unit: tokens per authoring session, before proofs

claims.text: Run at test time, the Bend oracle needs the Bend toolchain on every learner's machine (J6); run only at authoring time, expected outputs are frozen and each `codelarpers test` can no longer draw fresh seeded inputs.
Sampled laws can miss a bug that only rare inputs expose, where a proof would rule it out; likely on stages whose interesting inputs are sparse.

evidence.source: property testing samples, it does not prove

questions.ask: Do you want codelarpers to host courses where the learner writes Bend (a Bend starter kit), or only courses in languages like Rust, Python and Go?
questions.answer: No Bend courses. The user wants to know whether Bend can make agent-written test cases and submission checks stricter or better.
